solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Miss doing admin work?

parts.note: Miss is the title of a young unmarried woman, and one doing clerical jobs in a workplace is the answer; the pun is on miss as a failure

explanation.surface: Someone fails to hit a target while busy with paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a verb (to fail to hit), but it is the title for a young woman, here one employed for clerical duties.
explanation.definitionFit: A young woman employed in clerical duties is an old-fashioned term for a junior office worker.

clue.text: It can replace spinach or pine

parts.note: to pine or ache for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: Something can stand in for spinach or for a pine tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pine' looks like the tree, but here it is the verb meaning long for.
explanation.definitionFit: Orache, or mountain spinach, is a leafy plant cooked and eaten as a substitute for spinach.

clue.text: Build a total, perhaps

definitions.meaning: build here is the noun for a person's physique or shape
a total is an example of a number, a numerical amount

explanation.surface: Someone constructs a sum, maybe.
explanation.definitionFit: Physique is one sense of this noun; a number such as a sum total is another.

clue.text: Sadly, the last race in my 4×4?

indicators.note: in says the shuffled letters go inside the word for my

parts.note: cor is an exclamation like 'my!' expressing surprise

indicators.note: sadly says the following words are badly or regrettably rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone laments a final race run in their off-road vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: COR, the British exclamation of surprise, goes around the anagram of THE LAST RACE. A Chelsea tractor is a jokey British term for a big four-wheel drive driven in wealthy London districts.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase mocks four-wheel-drive SUVs used only for city driving in affluent parts of London.

clue.text: Find Bob wrapping hot pants

indicators.note: wrapping says the singer's surname goes around the other letters

parts.note: Bob Geldof is the Irish musician behind Live Aid

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish or poor, signalling the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Bob is wrapping up a pair of hot pants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot pants' looks like a garment, but 'pants' signals an anagram of HOT. Bob Geldof is the musician who organised Live Aid.
explanation.definitionFit: To obtain or track something down, as in to find a copy.

clue.text: Harsh soldier's shut outside

indicators.note: outside means the word for shut sits round the soldier

parts.note: to be shut of something is dialect for being rid of it
GI is an American soldier; the 's stands for is and links

explanation.surface: A soldier is locked out and treated severely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut' is from the northern British phrase 'shut of', meaning rid of.
explanation.definitionFit: A severe or inflexible regime is stiff and unbending, which is the sense here.

clue.text: Double points for turning round

indicators.note: turning round asks for the word for points to be read back to front

parts.note: tips are points or ends, as of pencils

explanation.surface: A dart scoring twice its value for spinning around.
explanation.walkthrough: A spit, as in 'the spit of his father' or 'spitting image', is an exact likeness. The surface also hints at a roasting spit, which turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, someone who is the very spit of another is their exact likeness or lookalike.

clue.text: Charges into battle?

parts.note: charges are prices, and turning them into a battle between sellers cutting them is the answer

explanation.surface: Troops rushing headlong into a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' looks like a cavalry attack, but it means prices, which rival shops fight over.
explanation.definitionFit: Competing sellers repeatedly cutting what they ask for goods wage this kind of commercial fight.

clue.text: Sensible, so she's moved

definitions.meaning: someone level-headed and well organised is described this way
split 2,3,3 the answer means in order to affect a lady, so that she is moved emotionally

explanation.surface: A woman is touched because the act was so level-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as TO GET HER, the answer means 'in order to move her'; 'get' can mean to affect emotionally.
explanation.definitionFit: A composed, well-organised person is informally said to have it all in place, the sense here.

clue.text: Being dishonest about imaginary cat is OK

indicators.note: about means the word for cheating goes around the other pieces

parts.note: fiddling is cheating, as in fiddling the books
air as in air guitar, an imaginary instrument
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: Cheating over an invented pet is deemed acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air' means imaginary as in air guitar, played on an instrument that is not there.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something middling, neither good nor bad, just acceptable.

clue.text: Fish? That could be right

definitions.meaning: to fish with a rod and line is to go angling
a right one of ninety degrees is an example of the answer, the corner made by two lines

explanation.surface: Someone half-recognises a fish and guesses it may be the correct one.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishing with rod and line is a verb sense; a right one is a ninety-degree example of the geometric sense.

clue.text: Shut bars for measurement of insulation

parts.note: a door pushed to is shut
a grating is a framework of bars

explanation.surface: Closing a set of bars as part of an insulation test.
explanation.walkthrough: The tog rating is the British scale for how warm a duvet or garment is.
explanation.definitionFit: The tog is a unit of thermal resistance, so the figure measures how well bedding insulates.

clue.text: I start to offer toast — the rest offer sandwiches

indicators.note: the phrase the rest offer holds the answer between its outer letters like a filling

explanation.surface: One person begins the toasts while everyone else hands round sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' looks like food at a party, but it says the answer sits inside 'the rest offer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying these words is the conventional opening for proposing a toast to someone.

clue.text: River suffered when abandoned by international organisation

indicators.note: abandoned by says the organisation's letters leave the word for suffered

parts.note: to have undergone something is to have suffered it
UN is the United Nations

explanation.surface: A river was hard done by after an international body pulled out.
explanation.walkthrough: The Derwent is the name of several English rivers, including one in Derbyshire and one in the Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: Several rivers in England and one in Tasmania bear this name.

clue.text: Virgin Atlantic trip?

parts.note: virgin suggests a first-ever sailing, and an Atlantic crossing is a typical ship's journey, rather than a flight with the airline

explanation.surface: A flight with the airline Virgin Atlantic.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital V makes you think of Richard Branson's airline, but the clue means a ship's very first crossing, like the Titanic's.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's first journey after launch is described with a word meaning virgin or first.

clue.text: Want to get seen turning over feasts

indicators.note: over means the reversed word covers, going round, the word for feasts
turning says the word seen is read backwards

parts.note: to dine is to feast

explanation.surface: Someone longs to be noticed going back over banquets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Want' looks like a verb meaning desire, but it is the noun meaning poverty.
explanation.definitionFit: Want, as a noun, is poverty or lack, which is the state of being poor.

clue.text: Country folk admitting old game's a mess

indicators.note: admitting means the country folk let the other letters in

parts.note: hicks are rustic country people
RL is rugby league; the 's stands for is and links

explanation.surface: Rustics let in an old game and it becomes a shambles.
explanation.walkthrough: Horlicks is a British malted milk drink, and 'make a horlicks of' is British slang for making a mess, a polite form of 'bollocks'.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, making a dog's dinner of something is to botch it, giving this sense of a shambles.

clue.text: Word image, not with letters represented

definitions.text: Word image, not with letters represented

indicators.note: not says the abbreviation must be taken away from the pool of letters
the letters of the phrase are represented in a new order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A picture of a word, shown without using any letters.
explanation.walkthrough: Take W (with) from the letters of WORD IMAGE and rearrange the rest; the whole clue also describes the answer, a symbol standing for a word rather than spelt.
explanation.definitionFit: A written character that stands for an idea or word, as in Chinese script, rather than spelling it out.

clue.text: Award briefly held by some

parts.note: the honour's short form OM sits inside the word some, and it is held at any time by only a few people

explanation.surface: A prize that a handful of people get to hold for a short while.
explanation.walkthrough: The British honour is abbreviated OM, and those two letters are held inside 'some'; membership is also limited to 24 people, so only some hold it.
explanation.definitionFit: This British honour, given by the monarch for distinguished service, is limited to twenty-four living members.

clue.text: Make swimmers use very deep jumps up in this

indicators.note: in says the reversed word sits inside the word for very

parts.note: so means very, as in so good

indicators.note: in a down entry, jumping up means the word deep is read from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Swimmers are made to dive very deep in this outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: Speedo is a brand of swimwear. 'Make' is the noun meaning brand, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: This brand name for swimwear is a manufacturer whose trunks and costumes swimmers wear.

clue.text: Mothball that woman left on empty valise

parts.note: she refers to that woman

indicators.note: empty removes the inside of valise, leaving its outer letters

explanation.surface: She packs mothballs in a suitcase that has been emptied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mothball' looks like the moth-repellent, but it is the verb meaning put aside for later.
explanation.definitionFit: To mothball a plan is to put it into storage and postpone it indefinitely.

clue.text: Working with copper to break up party for wild kid

indicators.note: breaking up the party means splitting its letters around the others

parts.note: Lib is short for the Liberal party
a machine that is on is working
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A police officer on duty breaks up a party to deal with an unruly youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a police officer and 'wild kid' like a tearaway; here they are the metal and a young animal of the wild.
explanation.definitionFit: A young offspring of the big cat, a wild animal, is called this.

clue.text: Resist love for young man

parts.note: to buck a trend is to resist it
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Someone holds out against romance on behalf of a youth.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an informal, chiefly Irish, form of address for a lad or young fellow.

clue.text: Home Office finally search comprehensive

parts.note: someone at home is in
a dept is a department, an office of government

indicators.note: finally picks only the closing letter of search

explanation.surface: The Home Office conducts a thorough search at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home Office' looks like the British government ministry, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A study covering every detail is thorough, or comprehensive.

clue.text: Border crossing contact is concern

indicators.note: crossing here means the word for concern lies across, around, the word for contact

parts.note: care is concern or worry
touch is contact

explanation.surface: Touching at a frontier crossing raises concerns.
explanation.walkthrough: A cartouche is an ornamental frame, especially the oval ring around a pharaoh's name in hieroglyphs.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an ornamental frame or scroll-shaped surround, which edges or borders what it encloses.

clue.text: One has to make hands perfect

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
to deal is to give out the cards that make up the players' hands

explanation.surface: Someone must shape their hands until they are flawless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hands' are not body parts but sets of cards; dealing is what creates them.
explanation.definitionFit: Something flawless and exactly as wished for is described by this adjective.

clue.text: House some of these migrants

indicators.note: some of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some of these incomers have found accommodation.
explanation.walkthrough: A semi is British shorthand for a semi-detached house, one sharing a wall with its neighbour.
explanation.definitionFit: British shorthand for a semi-detached dwelling, one of a joined pair.

clue.text: Bishop of Rome converted, embracing close to witness

indicators.note: embracing says the rearranged city wraps around the other pieces
converted asks for the letters of the city to be rearranged

parts.note: something on a building is close to it, as in on the coast
to sign as a witness, as at a wedding

explanation.surface: A Pope who changes faith while hugging someone near a witness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bishop of Rome' reads as the Pope, but 'Bishop' alone is the definition; 'of' only links it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: This Italian honorific title is used for prelates, including bishops, in the Catholic church.
